cues.text: A Distinguished Teacher at Reims
Born around 1030 in Cologne, Bruno studied and later taught theology at the cathedral school of Reims , becoming one of the most respected teachers in France.
Among his students was a young cleric named Odo of Châtillon, who would later become Pope Urban II.
Bruno rose to become chancellor of the diocese of Reims, a position of real influence and comfort.
A Turn Toward Solitude
Disturbed by corruption he encountered in the archdiocese and drawn increasingly toward a life of contemplative prayer, Bruno resigned his position around 1080.
Together with a small group of companions, he sought out St. Hugh of Grenoble , a bishop renowned for his own holiness, to help them find a place suited to an eremitical life.
Founding the Grande Chartreuse
In 1084, Hugh led Bruno and six companions into a remote, rugged Alpine valley called the Chartreuse , north of Grenoble.
There, they built simple individual cells around a small chapel and lived in near-total silence.
They were given over to prayer, manual labor, and the copying of manuscripts, meeting together only for essential common worship.
Bruno wrote no formal rule, believing instead that his own example of a life 'hidden in the Face of God' would be guide enough for those who followed him.
Called to Rome and Back to Solitude
In 1090, Bruno's former student, now Pope Urban II , summoned him to Rome to serve as an advisor in the ongoing work of Church reform.
Bruno obeyed but found the noise and business of the papal court deeply uncongenial to the solitary life he had built.
After twice declining offered bishoprics, he persuaded Urban to release him to resume eremitical life.
He founded a second small community, St. Mary's at La Torre, in Calabria, southern Italy.
Final Years and Death

Bruno spent his last years at La Torre in prayer and study, composing commentaries on the Psalms and the Epistles of St. Paul, and remaining close to Count Roger of Sicily, who had granted the community its land.
He died there on October 6, 1101, having outlived, within a short span, his former student Pope Urban II, the first prior of the Grande Chartreuse, and his patron Count Roger.
Legacy
Though Bruno never intended to found a formal religious order, the community at the Grande Chartreuse grew into the Carthusian Order .
The order's distinctive combination of solitary cells with limited common worship was codified in writing only after Bruno's death by the order's fifth prior, Guigo.

Nine centuries later, the Carthusian Order remains one of the most austere and unchanged forms of religious life in the Catholic Church, still centered at the same mountain valley where Bruno first settled.
